intro: In 1882, a young teacher named Jigorō Kanō opened a small training room at a temple in Tokyo. Older fighting schools in Japan kept their lessons private. Kanō wanted lessons any school could share. He called his art judo.

Far away in England, boxers once fought with bare hands for prize money. In 1867, a page of twelve rules asked for gloves and timed rounds. In both places, a written code changed a rough fighting world into a sport with a start, an end and a referee.

In this unit, you will meet Kanō, his ranks and his ideas. You will compare judo's rules with the Queensberry Rules. By the end, you can explain how a rulebook helps a sport enter schools and the Olympics.
bigQuestion: How does writing rules down turn an old fighting practice into a school sport?

test.why: Jigorō Kanō founded judo at the Kodokan in 1882.

test.q: Where did the Kodokan first open?
test.why: Kanō opened the Kodokan at Eisho-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo.

choices: a school or line of teaching
test.why: A ryu was a school or line of teaching, often with private lessons.

choices: Kanō gave the first dan ranks.
test.why: In 1883, Kanō gave the first dan ranks to two students.

test.q: What were Kanō's three goals for judo?
choices: physical education, contest and training the mind
test.why: In 1889, Kanō named physical education, contest and training the mind.

test.q: Which rule did the Queensberry Rules add to boxing?
test.why: The Queensberry Rules set three-minute rounds with a minute of rest.

test.q: Whose name is on the Queensberry Rules?
choices: the backer, the Marquess of Queensberry
test.why: The rules carry the name of their backer, the Marquess of Queensberry.

test.q: When did judo join the Olympics?
test.why: Judo joined the Olympics at the 1964 Tokyo Games.

choices: the first Asian member of the IOC
test.why: Kanō was the first member from Asia on the International Olympic Committee.

test.q: Why does a judo referee say hajime?
test.why: Hajime means begin. It starts the match.

test.q: Which group writes the rules for world judo contests?
test.why: The International Judo Federation, founded in 1951, writes world judo rules.

test.q: When did women first win Olympic judo medals?
test.why: Women won Olympic judo medals for the first time in 1992 in Barcelona.

test.q: How did the 1868 Meiji Restoration affect jujutsu schools?
choices: It made them all Olympic sports.
Many lost students as Japan changed fast.
test.why: The samurai rank ended and many jujutsu schools lost students.

test.q: What did Executive Order 9066 in 1942 lead to?
choices: Japanese Americans being forced into camps
test.why: The order led to about 120,000 Japanese Americans being forced into camps.
